# The Data Flywheel

::: {.callout-question}

How does the system get better from its own experience?

:::

Until now the robot has been fixed. It senses, decides, and acts with whatever
model it shipped with, and it is exactly as capable on its thousandth day as on
its first. That changes here: the system stops being automation and starts being
AI, because it gets better at the job by doing the job.

The mechanism is a loop, and it is the same loop that keeps a child coming back.
When the child corrects the robot, praises it, or teaches it something new, she is
not just interacting. She is labeling data. What makes the robot engaging to teach
is exactly what makes it improve. The engagement loop and the data loop are one
loop, and seeing that is the whole chapter.

## The flywheel

The loop has four stages (@fig-flywheel). The robot collects
experience as it runs. A curator keeps the small fraction of it that is worth
learning from. That kept data trains an improved model, off the device, where
there is room and power to do it. The improved model deploys back to the robot,
which now collects better experience than before. Each turn makes the next turn
richer, which is what makes it a flywheel and not just a pipeline.

::: {#fig-flywheel fig-cap="**The data flywheel**: the robot collects experience, a curator keeps the informative fraction, an improved model is trained off-device and deployed back, and the better behavior collects better experience on the next turn." fig-alt="A four-stage cycle running clockwise: collect the robot's experience, curate to keep the informative few, adapt by training off-device, and deploy the improved model, which collects again. The center notes that engagement is collection and the loop spins only if each round's gain beats its cost."}
![](../assets/diagrams/flywheel.svg)
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Properties in tension**: adaptivity against privacy. The data that improves the
system is the same private data you were careful to keep.
:::

## Quality, not quantity

The instinct is to log everything and sort it out later. It is the wrong instinct,
and the memory chapter already said why: storage is bounded, recall slows, and
every kept episode of a child's life is a privacy liability. The flywheel does not
run on volume. It runs on the informativeness of what you keep, and that is the
curator's whole job. Call the fraction it keeps the data yield:

$$\text{data yield} = \frac{\text{episodes kept}}{\text{episodes collected}}$$

The yield is not free to choose. The bytes shipped each round have to fit the
upload link and the privacy budget:

$$(\text{episodes kept}) \times (\text{bytes per episode}) \le \text{egress budget}$$

That budget is the ceiling, and the curator's job is to spend it on the most
informative episodes it can find.

A good curator has a low data yield and a high hit rate: it discards the
thousandth ordinary success, which teaches nothing, and keeps the surprising
failure and the moment the child had to correct it, which teach a great deal. This
is active learning by another name, with a constraint: the curator runs on the
device and cannot see what the off-device model already knows, so it judges by
signals that need no such insight, a human correction, a surprise, a failure, the
marks of an episode at the edge of competence. Keeping the informative two percent beats
keeping all of it, because the model learns from the edges of its competence, not
from the middle where it was already right. The edges alone are a trap, though:
train on failures and corrections only and the model forgets what it already did
well. So the curated slice is mixed back with a representative sample of ordinary
experience, an anchor that holds the base distribution in place, and the model
sharpens at the edges without drifting in the middle.

## The cost of a turn

A flywheel is only worth spinning if each turn pays. A turn costs a round trip:
collect, curate, ship the kept data off the device, train, and deploy the result
back. That round trip is slow, measured in days, and it spends the privacy budget
every time data leaves, which is why what leaves is the curated minimum, derived
or featurized where it can be and consent-gated when it is a child's, never the
raw firehose the deployment chapter keeps on the device. Forgetting is coarser
here than in memory, too: once an episode has trained a model, removing it takes a
retrain, because weights do not forget on command, so a deletion request reaches
the training set and the next model, not the one already shipped. So the turn has to buy more than it costs: the improvement it buys has to be
worth what the round costs. There is no
clean inequality here, because the terms do not share units: the gain is a change
in the model's competence, while the cost is days of latency, dollars of compute,
bytes of privacy, and the bandwidth and energy to ship the improved model back. Weighing them is a judgment, and the honest version of it
names them all rather than hiding behind the accuracy number. When the gain
clears that bar the flywheel compounds and the robot pulls away from where it
started; when it does not, you have built an expensive data pipeline that drains
privacy for a model that barely moves. The curator is what tips that balance, because it raises the
improvement per byte shipped, which is the only term you fully control.

## Build

::: {.callout-build title="Log, curate, and measure the yield"}

Build the logger first: record episodes as the robot runs, each with whatever
signal stands in for a label, the child's correction or reaction. Then build the
curator: a rule or small model that scores each episode for how much it would
teach, and keeps only the top slice. Measure the data yield, the fraction kept,
and look at what it chose. Did it keep the informative episodes and drop the
repetitive ones?

The improvement half of the loop is slow and off-device, and it may not show
within a session, which is the real constraint. Use the provided logged episodes
and the offline retrain they came with: measure the improvement delta from
training on the curated slice versus the full log. If the curated slice does
nearly as well on a fraction of the data, you have measured the curator's worth.

:::

## What the number says

The first surprise is how low a good data yield is: a curator earning its keep
throws away the overwhelming majority of what the robot sees, because most of
experience is unremarkable. The second is that the small curated slice often
trains a model nearly as good as the full log would, sometimes better, because the
full log drowns the informative episodes in routine ones. The flywheel rewards
selectivity, not collection. And the moment you see that the episodes worth
keeping are the ones richest in detail about the child, you see why adaptivity and
privacy are the same decision wearing two hats.

## Read

The curator is active learning: choose the most informative examples to label and
learn from, rather than all of them. When the labels come from watching an expert,
the loop is imitation learning, and DAgger (Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell, 2011) is
the version that closes it by collecting data on the learner's own mistakes. The
broader stance, that curating and cleaning the data beats scaling it, is
data-centric AI; and learning from human reactions rather than fixed labels is the
idea behind RLHF.

::: {.callout-teaching}

- **Hook**: the engagement loop and the data loop are the same loop. Open with
  that, because it reframes every interaction in the book as data collection and
  makes the flywheel feel inevitable rather than bolted on.
- **Open question**: this may be too ambitious for a first kit. Decide whether to
  build the full loop or teach it as a concept plus a logging-only exercise with
  the retrain provided.
- **Watch**: keep quality ahead of quantity. The seductive wrong lesson is "collect
  more data"; the right one is "keep better data," and the data-yield number is how
  you keep students honest about it.

:::
